note: Vol. I No. 16 — the number that resumes publication after the suspension announced on 4 March, and says so in its first editorial line: the paper had come from St Louis. Its masthead number is what settles the missing week, No. 16 following No. 15 with no number skipped.

claims.normalized: Having received our expected [supply of pap]er from St. Lo[u]is, we are enabled [to resume] [the s]uspended pub[l]ication of the Democrat […] one week to publish.
claims.notes: THE OTHER END OF THE SUSPENSION, and between them the two notices close the question T-0312 was written to ask. On 4 March the Democrat announced it would be discontinued for a few weeks for want of paper and named Doct. J. T. Temple's stage line from St Louis as the arrangement that would end it (1834-03-04 c001); here the paper has arrived, the publication resumes, and the paper says it lost one week. ONE WEEK IS EXACTLY THE HOLE: 11 March 1834 carries no issue, and the masthead agrees — this number is Vol. I No. 16, the next after No. 15, so the sequence is unbroken and no printed number is missing from the deposit. The deposit's own manifest and validation notes say the same ('No March 11 issue is supplied; the printed sequence resumes March 18 with No. 16'), and the difference this claim makes is that the paper now says WHY. The Democrat skipped the week; the scan set has no hole. The column is interleaved with the Bank debate beside it.

[FE]ELING that we have been misrepresented by the nomination of this 'Great Con[v]ention' of eight Individuals, and being unwilling that our fellow-citizens in the other counties composing this District, should be deceived by the supposition of this nomination being the voice [o]f the people of Cook county: we therefore take this method to inform them to the contrary, and would therefore call a me[e]ting of our fellow-citizen[s] of Cook county, for an expression of their choice of a suitable candidate to represent the people of this District. claims.notes: THE EAGLE HOTEL IN CHICAGO, named as the room a county political meeting is called into — the only hotel the March 1834 Democrat names in the town itself, as against the taverns it names (Graves', and E. Wentworth's on Flag Creek eighteen miles out). Unplaced: the notice gives the name and nothing else. The date moves in the next issue, 1834-03-25 reprinting the same call for the 16th of April at the same house (claim c009 there), which is worth holding because it means the meeting was still ahead of the town at the end of the month.

claims.notes: THE SECOND PARTNERSHIP THIS MONTH'S DEMOCRAT DISSOLVES, after Brewster, Hogan & Co. — and like that one it is a succession rather than a closure, Charles Taylor continuing the business alone. The trade is not stated in the notice and is not guessed at. H. S. Handy is the Maj. H. S. Handy who handles tickets for the Infant School benefit a week later (1834-03-25 c001), which is how a name in a dissolution notice becomes a person in the town. The surname is set 'MANDY' by this column's Tesseract fallback and 'HANDY' in the 1834-03-25 reprint of the same notice; the latter is the reading, and the former is left in the quote where it belongs.

claims.notes: A COURT HOUSE IN THE TOWN OF CHICAGO, named as the place the May 1834 term will be holden — the kind of building a reconstruction needs a date for, and this is one. It also puts a dwelling house and improvement on a described quarter section outside the town, which is section-and-range and not a town lot, so nothing here places anything on the plat. The two officers named are the county's: Stephen Forbes as sheriff and Richard J. Hamilton as clerk of the circuit court, the same Hamilton who signs the estray notice in this column and presides over the Infant School board a week later (1834-03-25 c001). 'RICH'D. 1. HAMILTON' is the column's misreading of the middle initial and the normalized reading takes J from the 1834-03-25 printing.

claims.normalized: [Wanted, TW]O or THREE Journeymen Cabinet Ma[k]ers, to who[m] [good] wages will be paid by W. REED. Chicago, Dec. 11, 183[3].
claims.notes: A SECOND CABINET SHOP IN THE TOWN, hiring — two or three journeymen wanted at good wages, which is a demand for skilled labour in a town of a few hundred people and the sharpest thing this month's Democrat says about the building trades. Read against A. Filer & Co.'s new manufactory on South Water street (1834-03-04 c005), the town supports two cabinet makers by March 1834. AND ONE OF THEM IS SELLING UP A WEEK LATER: 1834-03-25 (c008 there) auctions three cabinet benches, a full set of cabinet tools and cherry lumber at the shop of [W.] Reed, without reserve, which is a contradiction recorded on that claim and not on this one. The dateline year prints as 1839, which cannot be right in a Vol. I issue; 1833 is taken, and the misprint is left in the quote.

claims.notes: FOUR MAILS A WEEK INTO THE TOWN AND THREE OUT, over the postmaster's own signature — eastern on Wednesday, western, northern and southern on Tuesday, all departing Thursday but the southern, which goes Saturday. This is the traffic the town's roads carried in March 1834 and it is a small number: the whole outside world reaches Chicago on two days of the week. THIS IS THE HIT A LETTER-LIST SWEEP RETURNS IN THIS ISSUE AND IT IS NOT A LETTER LIST — the signature ends 'P. M.' but the notice is the office's timetable, exactly as the Chicago American's post-office matter was (T-0261). The month's one real list is in 1834-03-04, claims c024 and c025 there. Hogan is the same John S. C. Hogan who took over Brewster, Hogan & Co.'s stand in the same month.

claims.notes: THE TOWN'S PRICE CURRENT IS COMPILED BY A SOUTH WATER STREET STOREKEEPER — P. F. Peck, whose own card heads itself with the corner of LaSalle and South Water streets (1834-03-04 c019). Only the head of the table is claimed: the columns below it are a numeric table the segmenter has shuffled through two adjacent columns, and quoting figures out of it would be quoting the shuffle. What the head carries is the fact worth having, that the Democrat printed a weekly corrected price current from March 1834 and named the man who made it. The full table is a page-image job.

claims.normalized: KEPT BY [… ] [Chica]go — Illinois. [… ] has taken that noted Tavern [… ] lately occupied by Mr. [… ] [… ] he will make every possible [exertion to make it] the Traveller's Home.
claims.notes: A 'BUILDING LATELY OCCUPIED BY' CHAIN, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHAT THE EPIC ASKS FOR, and it arrives with both names destroyed. A noted tavern has changed hands: the new keeper's name is set as 'B UTQBRSOwL' by this Tesseract fallback column and the previous occupant's as 'Mr. Ii.', and NEITHER IS SUPPLIED HERE — a supply would be an invention, and the rule is that '[…]' marks absence. What survives and is worth keeping is the SHAPE: in the winter of 1833-34 a tavern already noted enough to be called so passed to a new keeper who advertised it as the Traveller's Home. The card is dated December 1833 in the adjacent fragment. A page-image read of page 4 column 3 would finish it, and that is a ticket rather than a guess. The column alternates with the boot and shoe card and the Athenian prospectus line by line.

claims.notes: A THIRD CORNER STORE ON SOUTH WATER STREET — at Clark — and this is the legible printing of it. The same advertisement stands in 1834-03-04 at page 3 column 5 and in 1834-03-25 at page 4 column 1, both through columns the segmenter broke to fragments, which is why the claim is made here and not there. With Peck at LaSalle (1834-03-04 c019) and Botsford at Dearborn and Lake (c014 there), the March 1834 Democrat gives THREE corner addresses on or off South Water within four blocks, which is the densest placement evidence this month yields.

claims.notes: THE SAME PIER TIMBER ADVERTISEMENT AS 1834-03-04 c004, AND IT DISAGREES WITH ITSELF ON THREE NUMBERS — 50-foot squared logs here against 30 there, 40 piles here against 50, 29 feet here against 25. Both columns are Tesseract fallbacks, so neither reading is senior, and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved: a reconstruction that wants the pier's scantlings has to read the page images, and until it does the two claims bracket the answer. WHAT BOTH AGREE ON is everything that matters most — 10,000 feet of oak squared a foot, 350 round tie logs of 24 feet squaring 11 inches, white oak piles squaring at least 12 inches, one third at the Piers by 15 April 1834 and the rest within the month, and poplar bought to float the oak rafts. This printing also gives the agent's initial cleanly as J. ALLEN, which 1834-03-04's column mangles. The proposals close on the 20th instant, and this issue is dated the 18th.
